segments.title: The Fog and What It Hides

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close reading of the novel many consider Dickens' greatest, and certainly his angriest.
Over the course of this series, we'll be moving through Bleak House chapter by chapter, unpacking its language, its fury, its comedy, and its heartbreak.
We begin today where Dickens himself begins — in fog.
To help us find our way through it, I have three remarkable guides.

Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads Bleak House as an anatomy of class power — every court, every slum, every act of so-called charity a mechanism for keeping the poor exactly where they are.
He brings the kind of controlled outrage the novel itself demands.

Prof. James Blackstone is a legal historian who knows Victorian institutions from the inside out — what the Court of Chancery actually was, how the Poor Law actually worked, what it meant in practice to be invisible to the state.
His dry wit and deep archive make him essential company.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice of more Dickens audiobooks than anyone alive — approaches the novel as a performer first.
He hears what the prose is doing before he thinks it — and his love for the grotesques and the gravely serious alike is, frankly, infectious.
Gentlemen — the fog.
The first word of Chapter One — not counting the title — is 'London.'
Just that. One word. One syllable. And then Dickens opens the throttle.
He gives us what I think is the most astonishing opening paragraph in the English novel — and I do not say that lightly.
He writes, and I need you to hear this at the pace it demands —
'Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping.'
'Fog on the Essex Marshes, fog on the Kentish heights. Fog creeping into the cabooses of collier-brigs; fog lying out on the yards, and hovering in the rigging of great ships.'
The repetition is liturgical — 'fog, fog, fog' — and yet it is not tedious for a single beat.
Because each fog is doing something different. It is creeping, hovering, lying — it is alive, and it is everywhere at once.
What strikes me every time is that the fog doesn't arrive neutrally — it arrives as a social condition.
Dickens moves the fog very deliberately down the social scale — from the open river, to the ships, to the streets, and finally into Chancery itself.
He writes: 'Fog everywhere; fog up the river... fog in the eyes and throats of ancient Greenwich pensioners, wheezing by the firesides of their wards.'
'Fog in the stem and bowl of the afternoon pipe of the wrathful skipper, down in his close cabin; fog cruelly pinching the toes and fingers of his shivering little 'prentice boy on deck.'
There is the skipper — comfortable, pipe, cabin — and there is the 'prentice boy on deck, shivering.
The fog is the same fog. But it falls differently on different bodies.
That is Dickens' argument in embryo, laid out before we have met a single character.
And then the fog finds its natural home — the Court of Chancery.
Dickens sets up the connection with a precision that looks like poetry but is actually jurisprudence.

He writes: 'Never can there come fog too thick, never can there come mud and mire too deep, to assort with the groping and floundering condition which this High Court of Chancery, most pestilent of hoary sinners, holds this day in the sight of heaven and earth.'
'Most pestilent of hoary sinners' — that is not a novelist's flourish. That is a verdict.
The real Court of Chancery in 1852, when Dickens was writing, had cases that had dragged on for forty, sixty years — the Jennings case ran over a century.
Families consumed, estates dissolved in costs, lives spent in waiting for a judgment that never came.
The fog isn't metaphor — or not only metaphor. It's also a documentary record of what that institution did to people.
What I love — and Daniel's point about the 'prentice boy crystallises this — is that the fog also functions as a kind of theatrical darkness.
In the theatre, when you want the audience not to see what's being set up, you bring the lights down.
Dickens brings the fog up — and under cover of it, he introduces us to Jarndyce and Jarndyce.
He describes it as a cause 'so complicated, that no man alive knows what it means.'
And the comedy of that — the absolute, pitiless comedy of it — is that the fog is the case and the case is the fog.
Neither can be seen through. Neither will ever clear.
That opacity is not accidental — it is the system's most important product.
When no one can understand what Jarndyce and Jarndyce means, who benefits?
The lawyers benefit. The officers of the court benefit. The parties to the suit are eaten alive.
Dickens names this directly when he says the suit has become 'so costly as to be, in some sort, a monument of Chancery practice.'
A monument. Not a failure of the system — a monument to it. The fog is the point.
And Dickens was writing with receipts, as they say now.
There are scholars who've traced Jarndyce and Jarndyce to at least three or four real Chancery suits Dickens would have known — including one touching his own family.
The detail he gives is forensic — the 'mountains of costly nonsense,' the 'ruin of suitors,' the 'interminable suits' that 'exhaust finances, patience, courage, hope.'
These are not rhetorical inventions. They are transcriptions of what anyone reading the law reports of the 1840s would recognise immediately.
The fog is also, to use a rather unglamorous word — evidence.
So from the very first paragraph, Dickens has given us atmosphere, social argument, and a legal indictment — all inseparable, all wrapped in fog.
And lurking inside that fog, of course, are the people — some of the most extraordinary characters in Victorian fiction.
In a moment, we'll step inside the Court itself — and meet the Jarndyce and Jarndyce suitors, Esther Summerson, and the formidable cast Dickens assembles in those opening chapters.
Stay with us.
Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens' most ambitious novel apart — slowly, carefully, and with genuine pleasure.
I'm your host, and today we begin a deep dive into one of the great obsessions of Bleak House: the secret, and what it costs.

Lady Dedlock's hidden past, Esther's unknown parentage, Tulkinghorn's cabinet of other people's shame — this is a novel where concealment is both the engine of the plot and a kind of moral indictment.
With me today are three people who know this book as well as anyone alive.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads Bleak House as an anatomy of class power — and who will not let us forget what the system is actually protecting when it keeps its secrets.
Prof. James Blackstone brings the historical reality — what these institutions actually were, what the law could and could not do, and who paid the price when it failed.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice of more Dickens audiobooks than any other living human — who hears in every sentence what Dickens meant it to sound like.
Daniel, let's begin with you — because the central secret of Bleak House isn't really Lady Dedlock's, is it?
No — and that's exactly the right place to start.
Lady Dedlock's secret is the one we follow through the plot, but the deeper secret — the one Dickens is anatomising — is institutional.
Chancery's secret is that it serves no one it pretends to serve.
Look at the very opening of the novel — the fog, the mud, the Court of Chancery sitting in the heart of it.
Dickens writes: 'Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping.'
That fog is not decorative.
It is the atmosphere that the system requires — pervasive, undiscriminating, choking.
The fog hides nothing from Dickens and everything from the people trapped inside it.
That fog passage is one of the most precise pieces of social criticism in all of Victorian literature, and I want to insist on that word — precise.
Chancery in 1852 was genuinely, historically, a court that could hold a case in perpetuity.
Jarndyce and Jarndyce is satirical, yes — but only slightly exaggerated.
There were real cases lasting generations, real estates devoured entirely by legal costs.
And here is the secret that Dickens exposes: the court's purpose was never resolution.
Its purpose was continuation — because continuation meant fees, and fees meant power, and power meant that the lawyers and the masters of the court lived very comfortably indeed.
James has put his finger on something important, but I want to add the texture of it — because Dickens doesn't just expose that secret, he performs it.
Think of the very first paragraph of the novel in Chancery's chapter — that extraordinary rolling catalogue.
'Never can there come fog too thick, never can there come mud and mire too deep, to assort with the groping and floundering condition of this High Court of Chancery.'
'Groping and floundering' — those are not metaphors chosen by accident.
They are verbs of deliberate, systemic confusion — and they sound deliberate when you read them aloud.
Dickens was a superb public reader of his own work, and this prose is written for the voice.
The system gropes and flounders — and so do the people inside it.
And the people most completely destroyed by that floundering are never the wealthy wards of Chancery — they're the peripheral figures who never had standing to begin with.
Richard Carstone is ruined — but Richard is a gentleman, a Jarndyce heir.
His ruin is the novel's most sustained character study, but the system's deepest secret is what it does to Jo — the crossing-sweeper.
Jo doesn't know anything, understands nothing of Chancery, has never heard of Jarndyce — and yet the system touches him, corrupts the air around him, kills him.
That is the secret the fog is covering: not Lady Dedlock's past, but Jo's present.
Jo is someone we'll return to in depth — but I want to stay for a moment with the architecture of concealment, because Dickens builds it at every level of the social world.
James — Tulkinghorn.
Tulkinghorn is, I think, the most frightening figure in the novel — more frightening than any of the Chancery machinery.
Because he has no institutional mandate for what he does.
He is the Dedlock family solicitor, and he has, over decades, accumulated the secrets of every great family he has served.
Dickens gives us this extraordinary description of him — closed, dry, rusty, secretive.
'He is of what is called the old school — a phrase generally meaning any school that seems never to have been young.'
That sentence is a masterpiece of compressed social history.
The 'old school' is the code by which power preserves itself — by claiming that things have always been done this way, that change is vulgarity, that secrecy is simply discretion.
Tulkinghorn weaponizes that respectability — and the weapon is always information.
He is extraordinary to inhabit as a reader — a genuine pleasure, in the darkest possible sense.
Dickens never lets Tulkinghorn raise his voice, never lets him threaten openly.
The menace is in the flatness — in that old, measured, legal calm.
There is a scene — and I read this cold every time, knowing what's coming — when he confronts Lady Dedlock with the knowledge of her secret.
He tells her he has no intention of using the information — yet.
And then Dickens writes of him: 'He has his hand upon the key, and will put it in the lock, when he chooses, when he pleases.'
That repetition — 'when he chooses, when he pleases' — is the grammar of absolute power.
It is not cruelty, precisely — it is sovereignty.
Oliver's word — sovereignty — is exactly right, and it illuminates the class mechanics of the whole secret-keeping structure.
Tulkinghorn holds secrets about the aristocracy — but he uses them to preserve the aristocracy's position, not to challenge it.
His threat to Lady Dedlock is never 'I will expose you to the public' — it is 'I will manage you.'
The secret is a tool of containment — scandal must be prevented not for Lady Dedlock's sake, but for the sake of the class order she represents.
And this is what Dickens understands that no other novelist of his era quite grasps: the secret is never personal — it is always structural.
I want to bring Esther into this — because she is, in a sense, the secret that the novel gives us as its narrator.
Oliver — you've read Esther's voice hundreds of times.
What does Dickens hide inside her narration?
Esther is — and I mean this as the highest compliment — the most sophisticated unreliable narrator in Victorian fiction.
She doesn't lie — she deflects.
She has been trained from infancy to believe her very existence is a shame — her godmother-aunt tells her so, explicitly and brutally, on the night of her birthday.
And Dickens gives us that scene in Esther's voice, which means she gives us her own destruction with an eerie, practised calm.
'It would have been far better, little Esther, that you had had no birthday; that you had never been born!'
And Esther records this — without rage, without self-pity — as though it is simply part of the weather of her life.
That is the secret buried in her narration: she has internalised her own erasure.
And historically, that is precisely what happened to illegitimate children under Victorian law — they were erased.
'Filius nullius' — child of no one — was the legal designation.
No inheritance rights, no claim on a father's name, no legal personhood in any meaningful sense.
So when Esther's aunt tells her she would have been better unborn, she is not speaking pure cruelty — she is speaking the law.
She is telling Esther what the state has already decided about her.
And that is what makes Esther's narration so quietly devastating — because she has become her own censor.
She self-effaces in every paragraph — 'I don't know why I mention this,' 'I couldn't account for it,' 'I dare say I was wrong.'
Every one of those qualifications is a scar from that birthday scene.
The system doesn't need to silence her — it has taught her to silence herself.
We've been moving through different registers of secrecy — institutional, legal, personal — and they all seem to meet in one extraordinary character: Mr. Skimpole.
Because Skimpole's secret is perhaps the most insidious of all — he keeps it from himself.
Daniel — you've written about Skimpole as a portrait of something specific.
Skimpole is a portrait of liberal bad faith — and I use that phrase with absolute precision.
He presents himself as a child — innocent of money, innocent of consequence, floating beautifully above the sordid world of obligation.
He announces this with enormous charm, and Esther — good, trusting Esther — wants to believe him.
But the secret Skimpole keeps — keeps even from himself — is that his 'innocence' is simply a refusal to acknowledge the harm he causes.
He takes Jarndyce's hospitality, runs up debts that others pay, and — most damningly — accepts money from Bucket to betray Jo.
And Dickens gives him a kind of self-portrait that is a masterpiece of self-exculpating logic.
'I am a child. I know nothing of the matter. I never did know anything of the matter. And I never shall.'
The system's great secret is that it has room for Skimpole — room for charming, principled-sounding parasitism — because it needs people who will not look.
He is an absolute joy to read aloud — Dickens loads him with melody, with the cadences of a man performing his own enchantingness.
And the horror — when it lands — lands all the harder for the prettiness of the music.
Because we see what Esther cannot quite bring herself to see — that the charm is the mechanism.
There's a historical parallel worth pressing here — because the philanthropic class of the 1850s was full of Skimpoles.
People who made grand speeches about the condition of the poor while keeping their investments in the industries that produced that poverty.
Mrs. Jellyby is the more obvious target — telescopic philanthropy, Dickens calls it — but Skimpole is the sharper satire.
Because Skimpole's error isn't misplaced idealism — it is the comfortable decision not to know.
'The comfortable decision not to know' — that is a phrase worth sitting with.
Because it points to what this system requires above all: not active cruelty, but sustained, cultivated ignorance.
We'll return to the question of who is allowed to know and who is kept from knowing — and at what cost — after a short break.
But first — Oliver, one last thought on the architecture of secrets in this novel.
What strikes me most — as a performer, as someone who has lived inside this book for years — is that Dickens never lets the secret feel comfortable.
In other Victorian novels, the secret is a plot engine — it drives to revelation, revelation brings resolution, and we exhale.
In Bleak House, revelation brings nothing of the sort.
Lady Dedlock's secret is exposed — and she dies in the mud at the gate of a pauper's graveyard.
Jarndyce and Jarndyce is resolved — and the entire estate has been consumed in costs.
Dickens is telling us that revelation is not redemption — that exposing the secret doesn't dismantle the system that required it.
The fog, as he would say, is still everywhere.
The fog is still everywhere.
We'll be back after the break — and when we return, we go deeper into the novel's most unforgettable victim, and what it means that Dickens makes that victim a child who cannot read.

segments.title: Jo's London: Dirt, Disease, and the Law

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens' most ambitious novel apart — carefully, lovingly, and without mercy.
I'm your host, and today we're going deep into the city itself — the London that Jo the crossing-sweeper inhabits, and that the novel insists we look at directly.
Dirt, disease, and the law — three forces that shape Jo's world, and that Dickens wields like weapons against his comfortable readers.
To help us navigate that world, I'm delighted to welcome three extraordinary guides.

Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads Bleak House as an anatomy of class power — he'll make sure we understand exactly who benefits from Jo's misery, and who designed the system that produces it.

Professor James Blackstone is a legal historian specializing in Victorian institutions — he'll tell us what Chancery and the Poor Law actually were, and why Jo's experience of them was, devastatingly, entirely typical.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice of more Dickens audiobooks than anyone alive — will be our guide to the prose itself, to the rhythms and the rage built into every sentence.
Daniel, let's start with you — and with the mud.
The mud is the right place to start, because Dickens starts there — the very first paragraph of the novel plants us in London fog and mud so thick it seems to predate human civilization.
And that's not an accident of atmosphere — that mud is the accumulated waste of a city that doesn't know what to do with its poor.
Jo lives in Tom-all-Alone's, the ruined slum that the Court of Chancery has allowed to fester for decades because the legal dispute over its ownership has never been resolved.
The law doesn't just fail Jo — the law creates the conditions in which Jo exists.
Dickens makes this explicit — and it's one of his most devastating passages — when he turns to address Tom-all-Alone's directly.
"Tom has his revenge. Even the winds are his messengers, and they serve him in these hours of darkness. There is not a drop of Tom's corrupted blood but propagates infection and contagion somewhere."
Tom's revenge — meaning the slum's revenge on the society that created it and then looked away.
Disease doesn't respect class boundaries, and Dickens knows it.
That's the political argument buried in the epidemiology — you can't quarantine poverty forever.
And that argument had very specific, real-world force in the early 1850s when Dickens was writing.
The Broad Street cholera outbreak was only a year or two away from Bleak House's serialization — cholera had already killed tens of thousands in previous epidemics.
The miasma theory — the idea that disease arose from foul air and rot — meant that slums like Tom-all-Alone's weren't just moral embarrassments.
They were understood to be, quite literally, lethal to the surrounding city.
Now, as for Jo and the law — the crossing-sweeper's position is illuminating in a very precise way.
Jo knows almost nothing — that much the novel is at pains to establish.
But he does have one encounter with the legal system, when he's called as a witness — and the law promptly discovers he can't take an oath because he has no understanding of what an oath means.
So the system that has shaped his entire existence — shaped it brutally — simultaneously refuses to acknowledge that he exists within it.
That is not a Dickensian exaggeration — that is a fairly accurate description of how the law treated the destitute in the 1850s.
What James is describing — that legal exclusion — Dickens renders it in a passage that I find almost unbearable to read aloud, and I've read it perhaps two hundred times.
It's the passage where Dickens catalogues, with mounting fury, everything Jo doesn't know.
"He knows that it's hard to keep the mud off the crossing in dirty weather, and harder still to live by doing it. Nobody taught him, even that much; he found it out."
He found it out — that's the phrase that gets me.
Everything Jo knows, he taught himself, in the mud, with no one's help — and what he's learned amounts to the bare minimum required to survive, which he barely does.
The prose rhythm there is doing something very specific — each clause is shorter than the one before it, tightening until you reach that bleak little verb: found.
Dickens was performing that boy's diminishment in the very structure of his sentences.
Oliver puts his finger on something important — the prose is doing political work at the level of syntax.
But I want to push further into the mechanics of how Jo is kept where he is — because it's not just neglect.
The police actively move Jo on — repeatedly — whenever he stops anywhere.
"Move on" is one of the novel's great refrain-phrases.
"Move on, Jo. It's always the same with you. You are never to stop anywhere."
The law, in the form of Bucket and the constables, doesn't incarcerate Jo — it does something crueler.
It keeps him in constant motion, exhausted, unable to rest, unable to belong anywhere — until he simply runs out of body.
The system doesn't need to formally exclude him — it just never lets him stop.
That practice had a formal name — the Vagrancy Act of 1824 effectively gave police the power to move on anyone deemed to be loitering.
A crossing-sweeper was in a permanently ambiguous legal position — technically providing a service, but perpetually at risk of being reclassified as a vagrant.
The legal category of the destitute person was essentially: someone who doesn't quite exist, and whom the state therefore has no obligation to.
The Poor Law offered the workhouse — which many would rather die than enter, and many did.
Jo never even reaches the threshold of the workhouse.
He's below that, in a category the Victorian state simply had no apparatus for addressing — which is to say, it had every apparatus for ignoring.
There's a scene I always think of when we talk about Jo and the law — his encounter with Snagsby, the law stationer, who gives him a half-crown.
Snagsby is one of Dickens' beautiful minor characters — genuinely kind, genuinely helpless.
He presses coins into Jo's hand with a regularity that is both touching and entirely futile.
Dickens writes — and this is a line I love for its bleak precision — of Snagsby being "in a manner, taken into custody" by Jo.
"In a manner, taken into custody by the spectre of Jo, and haunted by it."
Taken into custody — by the law's own language turned inside out.
Jo haunts the conscience that can't save him — and the word Dickens uses is spectre, which tells you everything about how the comfortable classes experienced the poor.
As an apparition — something glimpsed at the edge of vision, disturbing but insubstantial.
And yet Dickens refuses to let Jo be merely spectral — which is where the novel becomes genuinely radical.
Jo's death chapter — chapter forty-seven — is one of the most politically ferocious things Dickens ever wrote.
Jo dies learning the Lord's Prayer, taught by Woodcourt — and Dickens stops the scene dead and turns directly on his audience.
"Dead, your Majesty. Dead, my lords and gentlemen. Dead, Right Reverends and Wrong Reverends of every order. Dead, men and women, born with Heavenly compassion in your hearts."
"And dying thus around us every day."
That is not sentiment — that is an indictment.
Dickens names his readers — their Majesties, their lordships, their reverends — and charges them directly.
Jo's death is not a tragedy that happened — it is a crime that was committed, with the reader's connivance.
That passage becomes even more pointed when you know that Dickens had public health statistics directly in front of him.
The 1840s and 1850s saw the great sanitationist debates — Chadwick's reports, the General Board of Health, the first Public Health Act of 1848.

The data was there, the arguments were made, the mortality rates were published — and the political will to act was repeatedly blocked by vested interests and a deep ideological horror of state intervention.
Tom-all-Alone's is fictional — but there were dozens of Tom-all-Alone's in London, all documented, all known, all allowed to persist.
So when Dickens writes "dying thus around us every day," he means it literally — there were weekly mortality reports showing exactly that.
I've read that death chapter in front of an audience once — a live performance, at a theatre — and the silence afterward was unlike anything I've experienced on stage.
Not the silence of respect — the silence of shock.
Because what precedes it is so unbearably tender — Woodcourt guiding Jo through the Lord's Prayer, word by word.
"The light is come upon the dark benighted way. Dead!"
That exclamation mark after "Dead" is the most violent punctuation mark in Victorian literature, as far as I'm concerned.
It's not grief — it's accusation.
Grief sharpened into accusation — that feels like exactly the right note to sit with before we turn to our next thread.
We've been mapping Jo's London — the mud, the disease, the law that moves him on and refuses to see him.
And we've arrived at Dickens doing something remarkable — using the death of one illiterate child to put an entire society on trial.
Coming up, we'll look at how the novel's other great institutional force — Chancery itself — mirrors and magnifies everything Jo suffers.
Stay with us.
Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked — the show where we take Dickens' great fog-drenched masterpiece apart, chapter by chapter, and hold it up to the light.
Today we're turning our attention to Richard Carstone — the young ward of Chancery, cousin to Esther Summerson, and one of the most heartbreaking figures in the novel.
He begins the book as a charming, restless, golden young man — and by its end he is hollowed out.
The question we want to unpick today is: how does Chancery do it?
How does the suit of Jarndyce and Jarndyce consume a young life so completely — and what does Dickens want us to understand from watching it happen?

With me are three people who know this novel very well indeed: Daniel Rosen, who reads Bleak House as a precise anatomy of class power; James Blackstone, who brings the legal and institutional history alive; and Oliver Trevelyan, who has performed Dickens longer than anyone cares to admit and who hears this prose from the inside.
Daniel, let's start with you — because I suspect you see Richard's destruction not as personal tragedy but as something structural.
Structural is exactly the right word, and I think it's important we resist the temptation to read Richard as simply weak.
Weakness implies he could have chosen differently — as if willpower were the missing ingredient.
But Dickens shows us very carefully that Chancery is designed to do exactly this — to take whatever is vital in a person and redirect it toward itself.
Richard tries medicine, tries law, tries the army — and in every case the Jarndyce suit is the reason he can't commit.
Not because he's lazy — he's genuinely earnest in each attempt — but because the suit always offers a horizon that makes real work feel provisional.
Dickens gives us that terrible logic in Jarndyce's own words — and Jarndyce understands it better than anyone.
He warns Richard: 'Suffer any wrong that can be done you rather than come here.'
That line — spoken near the very opening — is the thesis of everything that follows for Richard.
And what's so devastating about that warning is that Richard hears it — he genuinely hears it — and it makes absolutely no difference.
Which is itself Dickens' point, I think.
The suit doesn't overpower Richard with brute force — it seduces him with the logic of the almost.
It's always about to resolve, always on the verge of releasing its treasure — and that 'almost' becomes his whole interior weather.
And Dickens renders that beautifully in the prose rhythms around Richard — there's a restlessness built into the very syntax of his scenes.
When Esther watches him, when she describes his bright eyes and his nervous energy, she's also describing someone whose mind can never quite settle.
The novel puts it with terrible precision when Esther reflects that Richard's attachment to the suit was 'not a doubt but a disease.'
'Not a doubt but a disease.'
Five words, and somehow they contain the whole of it.

And I'd want to anchor that disease in something concrete — because what Dickens understood, and what the historical record confirms, is that Chancery in the mid-nineteenth century was a genuinely pathological institution.
Cases routinely outlasted their original litigants by decades — sometimes by generations.
There was a real case — the Jennens case, which Dickens drew on — where the original plaintiff had been dead for over a century when the litigation was still active.
So when Dickens writes Richard believing that the suit will resolve in his favour within months — we recognise that as a delusion precisely calibrated to the institution.
Chancery didn't just delay justice — it manufactured hope as a by-product of delay.
And that manufactured hope is what Daniel is identifying as structural — it's not incidental cruelty, it's the machine working as designed.
Dickens captures that mechanism in the scene where Richard consults Vholes for the first time — Vholes, who is practically the embodiment of the system.
He describes Vholes as having 'a slow, sure, noiseless way with him, as if he were making hay of you.'
Making hay of you — quietly harvesting a human being.
Vholes is one of Dickens' most terrifying creations precisely because he's so respectable.
He has a father in the Vale of Taunton, he has three daughters — Dickens gives him all the trappings of domesticity, of a man with dependants.
And the novel points out explicitly that this is how the system justifies itself — every parasite has a family to feed, and the family becomes the moral alibi.

There's that devastating narratorial aside where Dickens writes about the Vholeses of the world as creatures that feed on suitors — and then immediately notes that we cannot abolish them because, after all, they have families.
He writes: 'The one great principle of the English law is to make business for itself.'
It's said with the flatness of a coroner's verdict — and it lands that way.
Richard doesn't just fall victim to a corrupt institution — he becomes its product, its yield.
Can I say something about Ada's function in all this — because I think she gets underread as merely the loving constant, the faithful wife?
But Dickens is doing something much sharper with her.
Ada herself is a ward in Jarndyce and Jarndyce — which means Richard's marriage to her is, in part, his way of marrying the suit.
He can't separate his love for Ada from his obsession with what he imagines the case will give them both.
And that's where the real tragedy is — the contamination of genuine feeling by institutional hope.
The moment that breaks me every time — and I've read it aloud many times — is near the end, when Richard is clearly dying and he still speaks of the suit turning in their favour.
He says to Ada: 'I have been thinking, Ada, that I am not so ill as to be quite unfit for business.'
Business — at the last — and you feel the word like a cold hand.
And what makes that moment historically precise is that Dickens understood exactly what late-stage litigation obsession looked like in practice.
There are records — court papers, family letters — from the period, describing heirs who spent inheritances pursuing claims that were already, by any rational measure, lost.
The sunk-cost logic of Chancery was a known pathology — not a metaphor Dickens invented, but a social reality he was documenting.
And the detail that Richard ultimately joins the proceedings as a party himself — not merely a ward but an active litigant — is the novel's clearest structural move.
That is the moment the institution fully captures him.
Jarndyce warns him with immense sadness — and Dickens renders that warning with the novel's characteristic dry ferocity.
He writes that the suit has 'stretched out its long, lean arm' to draw Richard in.
A long, lean arm — not a trap, not a snare, but something almost organic, patient, and hungry.
And I'd push on something Oliver raised — the question of whether Richard ever had a realistic exit.
Jarndyce himself manages — he's a ward of the same suit, and he survives it with his humanity intact.
But Jarndyce has already inherited — he has Bleak House, he has position, he has what Bourdieu might call the cultural capital to absorb the suit without being absorbed by it.
Richard has nothing but expectation — which means the suit is not a threat to his security but the entire foundation of it.
That's the class dimension the novel encodes very carefully — the suit destroys exactly the people who cannot afford to be destroyed.
Dickens writes of Richard — and this is a line I return to again and again — that he was 'the victim of a fatal habit of putting off.'
'The victim of a fatal habit of putting off.'
The word 'victim' is doing enormous work there — Dickens will not let us call it a character flaw without first calling it a wound.
And it's Ada who has to watch all of it — which Dickens stages with extraordinary cruelty and compassion in equal measure.
There's a chapter — I think it's in the later third of the novel — where Esther visits Richard and Ada in their lodgings, and the shabbiness of the rooms is rendered as a kind of indictment.
Richard is drawn, thin, bright-eyed with something that isn't health.
And Ada is trying — with this heartbreaking cheerfulness — to make the rooms feel like a home when they are clearly already a waiting room.
Dickens describes her in those scenes with a phrase that I think is one of the most quietly devastating things he ever wrote.
He writes that Ada had 'the sorrowing face of one who sees what she must not speak of.'
That last clause — 'what she must not speak of' — is the whole architecture of their marriage in eight words.
That phrase — 'what she must not speak of' — feels to me like one of the places where Dickens understands silences the way a playwright does.
And Richard's death, when it comes, doesn't feel like shock — it feels like a kind of terrible grammar completing itself.
The suit concludes, the costs consume the entire estate, and all that hope — all those years of waiting — resolves into nothing.

In our next segment, we'll follow the novel outward — from Richard's private ruin to the wider world Dickens builds around it: the streets, the slums, and the figure of Jo, who has no suit and no hope and yet illuminates everything.
Stay with us.

segments.title: Bleak House as Comedy and Cruelty

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the show where we take Dickens' longest, strangest, and perhaps greatest novel apart to see how it works.
I'm your host, and today we're turning to one of the novel's most distinctive and frankly unsettling qualities — the way comedy and cruelty are inseparable in Bleak House.
Dickens gives us some of the funniest characters in all of English fiction — and then deploys that comedy as a weapon.
With me today are three people who know this novel intimately and disagree about it in exactly the right ways.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian whose work on Victorian class structures has made him one of the sharpest readers of Dickens as a political novelist.
Prof. James Blackstone brings the legal historian's eye — he knows what Chancery actually was, what it cost, and who it destroyed.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the most prolific Dickens audiobook narrator alive — reads the novel as a performer first, and finds things in the prose the rest of us miss.
So — where does the comedy live in Bleak House, and what is Dickens doing with it?
The first thing to say is that the comedy in Bleak House is absolutely relentless — and I mean that as the highest possible praise.
You have Chadband — this magnificent, oleaginous fraud of a preacher — who speaks in a kind of holy gobbledygook that is one of the funniest sustained voices Dickens ever invented.
And then there's old Smallweed, who has to be shaken back into shape like a bag of loose parts whenever he gets too excited.
Dickens writes of Smallweed's wife, who he treats as a sort of human sandbag — he hurls cushions at her head and demands she be 'chucked.'
'Shake me up, Judy. Shake me up, you cat!'
It's pure music-hall — a horrible old man, and yet you're laughing even as you register that this couple is genuinely miserable.
That double register — delight and discomfort happening simultaneously — is the Dickens signature, and nowhere more so than here.
What I'd add is that the comedy is never innocent — it is always doing ideological work.
Take Mrs. Jellyby — a figure of tremendous satirical energy, a woman so consumed by her African philanthropic scheme that her own children fall downstairs and her household falls apart.
Dickens makes her absurd — and the laughs are genuine.
But the satirical target is a kind of charity that looks outward to distant suffering while the suffering at its feet goes unseen.
He writes that she has 'telescopic philanthropy' — her eyes can only focus at a distance.
'She could see nothing nearer than Africa.'
The joke is brilliant — but the point it lands on is serious: institutional charity serves the powerful by providing a moral alibi for neglecting the poor next door.
The legal grotesques work in precisely the same way, and here the historical record is rather bracing.
Tulkinghorn — Sir Leicester Dedlock's solicitor — is not a comic figure, exactly, but he is presented with an almost theatrical stillness that functions as a kind of dark comedy.
He accumulates secrets the way other men accumulate property — and the novel treats this as both monstrous and, in a horrible way, funny.
Chancery itself, of course, was a real institution — and the real Jarndyce and Jarndyce was probably the case of Jennens v. Jennens, which lasted over a century and consumed an entire estate.
Dickens gives Jarndyce and Jarndyce its famous epitaph in the opening chapter — and the comedy there is so black it becomes almost cosmic.
'Jarndyce and Jarndyce drones on. This scarecrow of a suit has, in course of time, become so complicated that no man alive knows what it means.'
A 'scarecrow of a suit' — that is the image of the English legal system.
Something to frighten birds away from the fields it claims to protect.
And what's so extraordinary from a performance perspective is the way Dickens modulates the comedy — he knows exactly when to turn the dial.
The Smallweed scenes are genuinely farcical — cushions flying, the granddaughter Judy expressionless, old Bart in his chair like a broken puppet.
But then the same Smallweed turns up as a creditor — a vulture at Trooper George's door — and the farce suddenly has teeth.
Chadband is perhaps the most purely comic creation in the book — his sermons are extraordinary nonsense, and Dickens lets you enjoy them fully.
He describes Chadband as 'a large yellow man, with a fat smile, and a general appearance of having a good deal of train oil in his system.'
'My friends, what is Peace? Is it war? No. Is it strife? No. Is it lovely, and gentle, and beautiful, and pleasant, and serene, and joyful? O yes!'
You can hear the congregation nodding — and you can hear Dickens absolutely despising every word of it, even as he writes it with such glee.
That tension Oliver identifies — the glee and the contempt operating together — is where I think the novel is most politically interesting.
Chadband isn't just a comic type — he is a specific kind of ideological operator, someone who turns poverty into a spiritual failing.
When he preaches at Jo — the crossing-sweeper, a child who cannot read, who has nowhere to sleep — the comedy curddles into something close to fury.
Dickens sets up the sermon with devastating precision — Chadband feeds at the table of the comfortable and then turns his unction on the starving.
'It is because you are in a state of darkness, because you are in a state of obscurity, because you are in a state of sinfulness, that I would rather address you.'
The cruelty is dressed in kindness — and the comedy is the vehicle for showing you exactly how that works.
There's a broader point here about what Dickens understood — almost instinctively — about how institutions sustain themselves through ritual absurdity.
The Court of Chancery in the 1850s really was a kind of theatrical performance — the wigs, the Latin, the interminable procedural delays.
It looked ridiculous, and the people inside it knew it looked ridiculous, and it ground on regardless.
Dickens renders this with the fog — that magnificent sustained metaphor from the very first page.
'Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping.'
And then he lands it: the Lord Chancellor sitting in Lincoln's Inn Hall at the very heart of the fog.
The comedy and the critique are the same gesture — the fog isn't just weather, it's the system's self-description.
What strikes me every time I read the novel aloud — and I've read it three times now in full — is how the comedy actually protects the reader.
Dickens is building toward some extraordinarily dark material — Jo's death, Esther's smallpox, the spontaneous combustion of Krook.
The comedy in the earlier chapters is doing the work of establishing trust — you laugh with Dickens, and then he takes you somewhere terrible, and you go.
Krook himself is a fascinating case — he is grotesque, almost pantomime, the rag-and-bottle warehouse presiding over a chaos of documents.
Dickens calls him the Lord Chancellor's double — his shop is a miniature Chancery, his ignorance a mirror of its impenetrable complexity.
And then Krook spontaneously combusts — and you realize the comedy has been preparing you for an image of the entire system consuming itself from within.
The joke and the prophecy were the same thing all along.
The spontaneous combustion is Dickens at his most politically audacious, I think.
The critics attacked him for it — Lewes, notably, called it a scientific impossibility — but Dickens defended it furiously, and I think he was right to.
Because what the spontaneous combustion is doing is imagining the system's terminal logic — the accumulated filth of Chancery producing heat until it ignites.
Dickens writes of Krook's end with a kind of savage glee: the grease on the windowsill, the smell in the air, the charred remains.
'Here is a small burnt patch of flooring; here is the tinder from a little bundle of burnt paper, but not so light as usual, seeming to be steeped in something.'
It is comedy as apocalypse — the grotesque made literal, the metaphor pushed until it explodes.
That phrase — 'comedy as apocalypse' — feels like it ought to be on the cover of every edition of this novel.
We've been talking about the comedy as a vehicle for critique — but there's another dimension here, which is the cruelty Dickens directs at his more sympathetic characters.
The suffering of Jo, of Esther, of Richard Carstone — that's not satirical cruelty, it's something else entirely.
We'll be picking up that thread — and the question of whether Dickens earns his pathos or tips into sentimentality — right after the break.

segments.title: Connected Fates: The Web of Obligation

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens' great fog-drenched masterpiece apart, scene by scene, character by character, to find out what makes it tick.
I'm your host, and today we're exploring one of the novel's deepest structural ideas — what we're calling the Web of Obligation.
Bleak House is a novel obsessed with connection — hidden connections, denied connections, connections that bind people together across every division of class and station.
Joining me today are three people who know this novel as well as anyone alive.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads Bleak House as an anatomy of class power — every institution a mechanism, every connection a potential trap.
Prof. James Blackstone is a legal historian who has spent his career mapping what Victorian institutions actually were and what they actually did to real people.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice of more Dickens audiobooks than anyone breathing — brings the ear of a performer to every sentence Dickens wrote.
The question before us today: what does it mean that in this novel, everyone is connected to everyone else — and that those connections are almost never a comfort?
The thing that strikes me first — and I've read this novel aloud in its entirety more times than is probably healthy — is that Dickens announces the web on the very first page.
He opens with fog.
And fog, in this novel, is not atmosphere for its own sake — it is a physical metaphor for everything that is obscured, entangled, and impossible to see clearly.
Dickens writes — and I never tire of this passage —
'Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping.'
That word 'defiled' — he doesn't just drift downstream, he arrives somewhere corrupted.
The fog connects the pastoral and the industrial, the clean and the filthy — and so does everything else in the novel.
Oliver is right about the fog, but I want to push on what it's actually connecting.
Because the web in Bleak House is not a neutral network of human relationships.
It is a system in which obligations flow downward and benefits flow upward.
Think about Jarndyce and Jarndyce — the suit that has been running for generations.
Everyone connected to it is consumed by it — but the lawyers and their clerks, Tulkinghorn, Vholes, are fed by it.
Dickens makes this explicit when he describes the case as something that has become so complicated that no living creature could understand it.
'This scarecrow of a suit has in course of time become so complicated that no man alive knows what it means.'
A scarecrow — something that looks like a person, frightens like a person, but has no life in it.
The web of obligation in this novel is very often a web that only appears to connect — it actually isolates.
Daniel's point about Jarndyce and Jarndyce deserves a moment of historical grounding, because Dickens wasn't exaggerating.
The Court of Chancery as Dickens depicts it in the early 1850s was genuinely one of the most dysfunctional institutions in English legal history.
Cases that ran for decades — the costs eventually devouring the entire estate under dispute.
So when Dickens writes of suitors who are ruined by hope, he is describing a documented social pathology.
Miss Flite is the perfect embodiment of it — a woman who has attended court every day for years, waiting for a judgment that will never come.
She names her birds — and this is the detail that undoes me every time — she names them Hope, Joy, Youth, Peace, Rest, Life, Dust, Ashes, Waste, Want, Ruin, Despair, Madness, Death.
'Hope, Joy, Youth, Peace, Rest, Life, Dust, Ashes, Waste, Want, Ruin, Despair, Madness, Death, Cunning, Folly, Words, Wigs, Rags, Sheepskin, Plunder, Precedent, Jargon, Gammon, and Spinach.'
The list begins in the human virtues and ends in legal absurdity — that is the arc of the novel in a single sentence.
James, when I read that list aloud — and I have read it to audiences who laugh and then go very quiet — the comic rhythm and the tragic content are perfectly calibrated.
Gammon and Spinach!
It's pure music-hall absurdism dropped into the middle of a list of human catastrophes.
But what I want to add to the web conversation is the question of what obligates people to stay in it.
Because the characters in Bleak House who suffer most are not there by accident — they're held by love, or loyalty, or the sheer impossibility of imagining any alternative.
Richard Carstone is the most devastating example.
Jarndyce himself warns him — in terms that are almost unbearably clear — that the suit will eat him alive.
'The system! I am tired of hearing of the system. It is not the system that ruins men, but men who ruin themselves by placing their hopes in the system.'
And Richard hears it, understands it, and is destroyed by the thing he cannot stop wanting.
Richard is important to me precisely because he's not poor.
He is a gentleman, a ward in Chancery, someone with theoretical claim on wealth — and the system still destroys him.
That tells you something about the reach of the web.
But I keep returning to Jo — the crossing sweeper — because he is the figure in whom the web becomes most visible, most brutal.
Jo is connected to almost everyone in the novel — Nemo, Lady Dedlock, Tulkinghorn, Esther, Bucket — and not one of those connections protects him.
Each one uses him or passes him on.
And then there is that passage — I think it is the most controlled piece of moral outrage in Victorian fiction.
'Jo lives — that is to say, Jo has not yet died — in a ruinous place known to the like of him by the name of Tom-all-Alone's.'
'That is to say, Jo has not yet died' — the correction is everything.
Merely surviving is the full extent of what this system permits Jo.
Tom-all-Alone's is one of the places where Dickens is absolutely precise about the mechanism of the web.
The slum exists because of the Jarndyce suit — it is property under dispute, therefore unmaintained, therefore falling into ruin, therefore breeding disease.
Dickens makes the causal chain explicit in a passage that reads more like a public health report than a novel.

'There is not a drop of Tom's corrupted blood but propagates infection and contagion somewhere. It shall pollute, this very night, the choice stream in which chemists on analysis would find the genuine nobility of a Norman house.'
The blood of the slum reaches the bloodstream of the aristocracy.
The web is not merely social or legal — it is biological, epidemiological.
And Dickens knew that in 1852 this was not metaphor — cholera did not respect class boundaries.
The epidemiological web is perhaps the most frightening one, but for me the most intimate version of it is Esther's.
Esther Summerson is connected to everyone, in every direction — she is illegitimate child, ward, nurse, friend, secret sharer — and she carries all of it with almost inhuman grace.
Until she literally catches Jo's disease.
Her connection to Jo — which is itself routed through Lady Dedlock's guilt and Jarndyce's charity — becomes bodily.
The web of obligation inscribes itself on her face.
She says it herself with that characteristic self-effacement that I find utterly devastating to perform —
'I was very ill indeed for many weeks. When I began to recover, I found my hair was gone, and that I should be quite different in appearance.'
'Quite different in appearance' — she can hardly bring herself to say it.
And what Dickens is doing is making the social wound visible on the one character who had most tried to be unmarked by it.
And yet Esther's disfigurement is also what triggers Lady Dedlock's final crisis — the connections don't stop, they cascade.
Lady Dedlock is herself a figure whose entire social position depends on the concealment of connection — her illegitimate child, her past life, her true self.
Tulkinghorn's power over her is the power of the web-keeper — someone who knows more of the threads than anyone else.
And he uses that knowledge not to help, not to heal — but to hold.
Dickens gives him a magnificent description — all those old-man's legs, all that dry parchment energy — but the key phrase is that he is 'mechanically faithful without attachment.'
'Mechanically faithful without attachment, and very jealous of the profit, privilege, and reputation of being master of the mysteries of great houses.'
The web, for Tulkinghorn, is property.
He owns connections the way a landlord owns houses — and extracts rent in the form of power.
That image of Tulkinghorn as a kind of knowledge landlord is one I find genuinely clarifying.
Because it maps onto a real Victorian phenomenon — the solicitor to great families who effectively held those families in a kind of permanent, legal dependency.
And what Dickens understands — and this is the deeply uncomfortable part — is that Inspector Bucket operates by the same logic.
Bucket is charming, efficient, occasionally even kind — but he too is a keeper and tracer of connections.
He finds people by following the threads of obligation — who owes whom, who knows whom, who has cause to fear whom.
Dickens puts it with that characteristic offhandedness that conceals real menace —
'Mr. Bucket of the Detective. That's my name.'
He identifies himself by his function, not his person — he is the detective, the follower of connections, as a matter of essential identity.
Bucket is one of the great delights of this novel to perform — that pointing forefinger, the genial warmth that is also a form of surveillance.
He's essentially the first fictional detective in English literature, and Dickens builds into him the deepest ambiguity about what detection means.
Is following the web of connection a form of justice or a form of control?
The answer the novel gives is: yes, and inextricably.
Even the best-intentioned characters — Jarndyce, Esther, Allan Woodcourt — cannot step outside the web.
What they can do — what the novel quietly argues for — is choose how to pull the threads.
That phrase — choose how to pull the threads — feels like the moral centre of everything we've been discussing.
The web is given — the question is what you do inside it.
We've moved from fog to Chancery to Tom-all-Alone's to Esther's scarred face to Bucket's pointing finger — and every stop on that journey has been a node in the same terrible network.
In our next segment, we'll look at what happens when the web tightens — the novel's great crisis points, and how Dickens handles them.
We've spent this episode deep inside the fog — Chancery's fog, London's fog, the fog of self-deception and institutional cruelty.
Before we close, I want to ask each of you the question the novel itself refuses to answer tidily.
Does the fog lift — and if not, what does Dickens leave us with?
Oliver, you've lived inside this book for so long — let's start with you.
The fog doesn't lift — not really.
Jarndyce and Jarndyce collapses, yes — the estate devours itself — but that's not resolution, that's just entropy.
What Dickens gives us at the end is something more complicated than hope.
Esther has her new Bleak House, her garden, her doctor husband — and she says something that has always stopped me cold.
"I have been shown the whole of my life, and know it to be beautiful."
Which is a genuinely moving line — and also, if you think about it for three seconds, a devastating one.
Because Esther has earned that beauty through suffering she never deserved — abandoned by her mother, disfigured by smallpox, denied her very name for most of her life.
The system didn't reform for her. She reformed around it.
That's the novel's central ideological manoeuvre, isn't it.
The suffering gets individualised — made into the texture of a single remarkable woman's character — while the machinery that produced the suffering continues to run.
Jo is dead. Gridley is dead. Richard Carstone is dead. Chancery killed them all.
And then Dickens pivots to Esther's rose-covered cottage and asks us to feel that something has been resolved.
But he can't quite do it. He's too honest for his own comfort.
Because he gives us Jo's death — that extraordinary passage — without any softening.
"Dead, your Majesty. Dead, my lords and gentlemen. Dead, Right Reverends and Wrong Reverends of every order."
That rhetoric isn't directed at Chancery alone. It's addressed to every governing class in England.
And then the sentence that always floors me: "And dying thus around us every day."
Every day. Not past tense. Present continuous. Dickens refuses to let it be history.
Daniel is absolutely right about the structural refusal there — and as a historian I find that passage almost unbearably precise.
Because in 1852, when Dickens is writing this, Jo is not a metaphor. Jo is a census category.
Tens of thousands of children in London — street-sweepers, mudlarks, crossing-boys — living exactly as Jo lives.
The fog in the novel's opening — that famous fog, coating everything, penetrating everywhere — is not merely atmospheric.
Dickens is describing something that was chemically real: coal smoke, effluent, the literal stench of a city that had no sewers adequate to its size.
And the opening of Chapter One has always struck me as one of the great acts of compressed social diagnosis in English prose.
"Fog everywhere. Fog up the river. Fog down the river. Fog on the Essex marshes, fog on the Kentish heights."
The repetition is doing forensic work there — it's mapping England geographically and morally at the same stroke.
And the fog, crucially, is always present tense. Always now. Never safely then.
James, you've just reminded me of something I think about every time I record that opening chapter.
When you read it aloud — when you actually put it in the air — the repetition of "fog" becomes something incantatory.
It's not description anymore. It's a kind of summoning.
Dickens knew this. He performed his own work — those famous public readings — and he always said that the thing had to breathe when spoken.
And what I find — after recording Bleak House more times than is probably healthy — is that the novel sounds more urgent now than it did when I first approached it.
The Chancery passages, the Dedlock passages — even the Smallweed scenes, which are farce of a very high order — they all have this undertow of accumulated rage.
Dickens the entertainer and Dickens the radical are not two different writers. They are the same voice.
I want to come back to what Oliver said about Esther — because I don't want to leave the impression that the novel simply neutralises her into sentiment.
Esther's narrative is actually subtler than it looks.
She is relentlessly self-deprecating throughout — "I know I am not clever," she keeps saying — but the effect is not humility.
The effect is a portrait of a woman who has been systematically taught to disappear — taught that she has no right to take up space.
Her aunt — the woman who raised her in cold piety — told her, as a child, that it would have been far better she had never been born.
And Dickens gives us this passage in Esther's retrospective voice — quietly devastating in its plainness.
"I had never heard my mama spoken of... I had never been shown my mama's grave... I had never been told why."
That triple "never" is the fog inside a person — the fog of withheld identity, of shame passed down like a bequest.
And what strikes me, placing all of this in its historical moment, is how accurate the fog metaphor remains.
The Great Stink of 1858 — London's sewage crisis that finally forced Parliament to act — was still six years away when Bleak House was published.
Dickens was writing in the knowledge that the crisis was visible, documented, and deliberately ignored.
That is what gives the novel its peculiar atmosphere of suffocating patience — nothing will be fixed because fixing it would disturb too many comfortable arrangements.
Chancery, in this reading, is not aberrant. It is exemplary.
I wonder, as we close — whether there's any sense in which the novel offers a way through.
Not a solution — none of you would allow me a solution — but a stance, perhaps, a way of holding oneself against the fog.
Oliver, a final word?
The way through — if there is one — is attention.
Dickens is the most attentive writer in the language — attentive to a crossing-sweeper's cough, to the way a greedy man moves his fingers, to the exact pitch of a lie.
And what the novel teaches — I think this is what it teaches — is that the fog persists partly because we agree not to see it clearly.
Esther sees. Jarndyce sees. Even Bucket — that extraordinary detective — sees, in his precise, morally compromised way.
And the novel says — quietly, firmly — here is what is in front of you.
"It is not denied by the young and old, the rich and poor, the wise and simple, all alike — it has been among us."
It has been among us. Full stop. No excuses tendered.
That's the novel's moral demand — not pity, not charity, not reform even — simply: see it.
Bleak House ends with Esther happy, or something very like happy — but the fog that opened the novel has never been formally declared lifted.
Daniel Rosen, James Blackstone, Oliver Trevelyan — thank you for seeing it so clearly with us today.
Bleak House Unpacked has been a production exploring one of the most urgent novels in the English language.
Whether the fog is Victorian London or something recognisably present — we leave that, as Dickens did, for you to decide.

c1:p5.text:
On such an afternoon, if ever, the Lord High Chancellor ought to be
sitting here—as here he is—with a foggy glory round his head,
softly fenced in with crimson cloth and curtains, addressed by a
large advocate with great whiskers, a little voice, and an
interminable brief, and outwardly directing his contemplation to the
lantern in the roof, where he can see nothing but fog. On such an
afternoon some score of members of the High Court of Chancery bar
ought to be—as here they are—mistily engaged in one of the ten
thousand stages of an endless cause, tripping one another up on
slippery precedents, groping knee-deep in technicalities, running
their goat-hair and horsehair warded heads against walls of words and
making a pretence of equity with serious faces, as players might. On
such an afternoon the various solicitors in the cause, some two or
three of whom have inherited it from their fathers, who made a
fortune by it, ought to be—as are they not?—ranged in a line, in a
long matted well (but you might look in vain for truth at the bottom
of it) between the registrar’s red table and the silk gowns, with
bills, cross-bills, answers, rejoinders, injunctions, affidavits,
issues, references to masters, masters’ reports, mountains of costly
nonsense, piled before them. Well may the court be dim, with wasting
candles here and there; well may the fog hang heavy in it, as if it
would never get out; well may the stained-glass windows lose their
colour and admit no light of day into the place; well may the
uninitiated from the streets, who peep in through the glass panes in
the door, be deterred from entrance by its owlish aspect and by the
drawl, languidly echoing to the roof from the padded dais where the
Lord High Chancellor looks into the lantern that has no light in it
and where the attendant wigs are all stuck in a fog-bank! This is the
Court of Chancery, which has its decaying houses and its blighted
lands in every shire, which has its worn-out lunatic in every
madhouse and its dead in every churchyard, which has its ruined
suitor with his slipshod heels and threadbare dress borrowing and
begging through the round of every man’s acquaintance, which gives to
monied might the means abundantly of wearying out the right, which so
exhausts finances, patience, courage, hope, so overthrows the brain
and breaks the heart, that there is not an honourable man among its
practitioners who would not give—who does not often give—the
warning, “Suffer any wrong that can be done you rather than come
here!”
c1:p5.summary: An extended satirical tableau of the Lord Chancellor and court staff in their fog-wrapped surroundings, processing endless technicalities while suitors are ruined financially and psychologically; Chancery has destroyed lives across the nation.

The old gentleman is rusty to look at, but is reputed to have made
good thrift out of aristocratic marriage settlements and aristocratic
wills, and to be very rich. He is surrounded by a mysterious halo of

parks among the growing timber and the fern, which perhaps hold fewer
noble secrets than walk abroad among men, shut up in the breast of

generally meaning any school that seems never to have been young—and
wears knee-breeches tied with ribbons, and gaiters or stockings. One
peculiarity of his black clothes and of his black stockings, be they
silk or worsted, is that they never shine. Mute, close, irresponsive
to any glancing light, his dress is like himself. He never converses
when not professionally consulted. He is found sometimes, speechless
but quite at home, at corners of dinner-tables in great country
houses and near doors of drawing-rooms, concerning which the
fashionable intelligence is eloquent, where everybody knows him and
where half the Peerage stops to say “How do you do, Mr. Tulkinghorn?”
He receives these salutations with gravity and buries them along with
the rest of his knowledge.

uncomfortable. I was so ashamed of my folly that I did not like to
confess it even to Ada, and that made me more uncomfortable still. I

lady’s confidence if I could have possibly declined it. It gave me
the most inconsistent opinions of her. At one time I thought she was
a story-teller, and at another time that she was the pink of truth.
Now I suspected that she was very cunning, next moment I believed her
honest Welsh heart to be perfectly innocent and simple. And after
all, what did it matter to me, and why did it matter to me? Why could
not I, going up to bed with my basket of keys, stop to sit down by
her fire and accommodate myself for a little while to her, at least
as well as to anybody else, and not trouble myself about the harmless
things she said to me? Impelled towards her, as I certainly was, for
I was very anxious that she should like me and was very glad indeed
that she did, why should I harp afterwards, with actual distress and
pain, on every word she said and weigh it over and over again in
twenty scales? Why was it so worrying to me to have her in our house,

better and safer somehow that she should be there than anywhere else?

It was not a love letter, though it expressed so much love, but was
written just as he would at any time have spoken to me. I saw his
face, and heard his voice, and felt the influence of his kind
protecting manner in every line. It addressed me as if our places
were reversed, as if all the good deeds had been mine and all the
feelings they had awakened his. It dwelt on my being young, and he
past the prime of life; on his having attained a ripe age, while I
was a child; on his writing to me with a silvered head, and knowing
all this so well as to set it in full before me for mature
deliberation. It told me that I would gain nothing by such a marriage
and lose nothing by rejecting it, for no new relation could enhance
the tenderness in which he held me, and whatever my decision was, he
was certain it would be right. But he had considered this step anew
since our late confidence and had decided on taking it, if it only
served to show me through one poor instance that the whole world
would readily unite to falsify the stern prediction of my childhood.
I was the last to know what happiness I could bestow upon him, but of
that he said no more, for I was always to remember that I owed him
nothing and that he was my debtor, and for very much. He had often
thought of our future, and foreseeing that the time must come, and
fearing that it might come soon, when Ada (now very nearly of age)
would leave us, and when our present mode of life must be broken up,
had become accustomed to reflect on this proposal. Thus he made it.
If I felt that I could ever give him the best right he could have to
be my protector, and if I felt that I could happily and justly become
the dear companion of his remaining life, superior to all lighter
chances and changes than death, even then he could not have me bind
myself irrevocably while this letter was yet so new to me, but even
then I must have ample time for reconsideration. In that case, or in
the opposite case, let him be unchanged in his old relation, in his
old manner, in the old name by which I called him. And as to his
bright Dame Durden and little housekeeper, she would ever be the
same, he knew.
c44:p33.summary: Esther recounts the substance of Jarndyce's letter: it is written with selfless love and deference; he emphasizes her youth versus his age, her disfigurement versus his devotion, that she owes him nothing, and that if she accepts, he asks only that she reconsider with time and remain as she is.

But not perceiving this quite plainly—only seeing it by halves in a

bad grace, and DO grumble very much. Then this respectability of Mr.
Vholes is brought into powerful play against them. “Repeal this

it, my dear sir? Never, with my consent. Alter this law, sir, and
what will be the effect of your rash proceeding on a class of
practitioners very worthily represented, allow me to say to you, by
the opposite attorney in the case, Mr. Vholes? Sir, that class of
practitioners would be swept from the face of the earth. Now you
cannot afford—I will say, the social system cannot afford—to lose
an order of men like Mr. Vholes. Diligent, persevering, steady, acute
in business. My dear sir, I understand your present feelings against
the existing state of things, which I grant to be a little hard in
your case; but I can never raise my voice for the demolition of a
class of men like Mr. Vholes.” The respectability of Mr. Vholes has
even been cited with crushing effect before Parliamentary committees,
as in the following blue minutes of a distinguished attorney’s
evidence. “Question (number five hundred and seventeen thousand eight
hundred and sixty-nine): If I understand you, these forms of practice
indisputably occasion delay? Answer: Yes, some delay. Question: And
great expense? Answer: Most assuredly they cannot be gone through for
nothing. Question: And unspeakable vexation? Answer: I am not
prepared to say that. They have never given ME any vexation; quite
the contrary. Question: But you think that their abolition would
damage a class of practitioners? Answer: I have no doubt of it.
Question: Can you instance any type of that class? Answer: Yes. I
would unhesitatingly mention Mr. Vholes. He would be ruined.
Question: Mr. Vholes is considered, in the profession, a respectable
man? Answer:”—which proved fatal to the inquiry for ten years—“Mr.
Vholes is considered, in the profession, a MOST respectable man.”
c39:p4.summary: Mr. Kenge's rhetorical defense of legal practitioners like Vholes is presented, along with a mock parliamentary inquiry that demonstrates how institutional self-interest defeats reform through the invocation of Vholes's respectable reputation.

Jo lives—that is to say, Jo has not yet died—in a ruinous place
known to the like of him by the name of Tom-all-Alone’s. It is a
black, dilapidated street, avoided by all decent people, where the
crazy houses were seized upon, when their decay was far advanced, by
some bold vagrants who after establishing their own possession took
to letting them out in lodgings. Now, these tumbling tenements
contain, by night, a swarm of misery. As on the ruined human wretch
vermin parasites appear, so these ruined shelters have bred a crowd
of foul existence that crawls in and out of gaps in walls and boards;
and coils itself to sleep, in maggot numbers, where the rain drips
in; and comes and goes, fetching and carrying fever and sowing more
evil in its every footprint than Lord Coodle, and Sir Thomas Doodle,
and the Duke of Foodle, and all the fine gentlemen in office, down to
Zoodle, shall set right in five hundred years—though born expressly
to do it.

“Hush! Hush!” The housekeeper looks round and answers in a frightened
whisper, “My Lady, I have not breathed a word of it, I don’t believe
what’s written in it, I know it can’t be true, I am sure and certain
that it is not true. But my son is in danger, and you must have a
heart to pity me. If you know of anything that is not known to
others, if you have any suspicion, if you have any clue at all, and
any reason for keeping it in your own breast, oh, my dear Lady, think
of me, and conquer that reason, and let it be known! This is the most
I consider possible. I know you are not a hard lady, but you go your
own way always without help, and you are not familiar with your
friends; and all who admire you—and all do—as a beautiful and
elegant lady, know you to be one far away from themselves who can’t
be approached close. My Lady, you may have some proud or angry
reasons for disdaining to utter something that you know; if so, pray,
oh, pray, think of a faithful servant whose whole life has been
passed in this family which she dearly loves, and relent, and help to
clear my son! My Lady, my good Lady,” the old housekeeper pleads with
genuine simplicity, “I am so humble in my place and you are by nature
so high and distant that you may not think what I feel for my child,
but I feel so much that I have come here to make so bold as to beg
and pray you not to be scornful of us if you can do us any right or
justice at this fearful time!”

But as it is wholesome that the parsimonious public should know what
has been doing, and still is doing, in this connexion, I mention here
that everything set forth in these pages concerning the Court of
Chancery is substantially true, and within the truth. The case of
Gridley is in no essential altered from one of actual occurrence,
made public by a disinterested person who was professionally
acquainted with the whole of the monstrous wrong from beginning to
end. At the present moment (August, 1853) there is a suit before the
court which was commenced nearly twenty years ago, in which from
thirty to forty counsel have been known to appear at one time, in
which costs have been incurred to the amount of seventy thousand
pounds, which is A FRIENDLY SUIT, and which is (I am assured) no
nearer to its termination now than when it was begun. There is
another well-known suit in Chancery, not yet decided, which was
commenced before the close of the last century and in which more than
double the amount of seventy thousand pounds has been swallowed up in
costs. If I wanted other authorities for Jarndyce and Jarndyce, I
could rain them on these pages, to the shame of—a parsimonious
public.
cP:p2.summary: Dickens asserts the factual basis of his Chancery depictions by citing real cases: a twenty-year suit with seventy thousand pounds in costs and another century-old suit with double that amount.

c15:p107.text:
“Mr. Jarndyce,” said Gridley with a rough sort of salutation, “you
bear your wrongs more quietly than I can bear mine. More than that, I
tell you—and I tell this gentleman, and these young ladies, if they
are friends of yours—that if I took my wrongs in any other way, I
should be driven mad! It is only by resenting them, and by revenging
them in my mind, and by angrily demanding the justice I never get,
that I am able to keep my wits together. It is only that!” he said,
speaking in a homely, rustic way and with great vehemence. “You may
tell me that I over-excite myself. I answer that it’s in my nature to
do it, under wrong, and I must do it. There’s nothing between doing
it, and sinking into the smiling state of the poor little mad woman
that haunts the court. If I was once to sit down under it, I should
become imbecile.”
c15:p107.summary: Gridley explains that his rage is essential to his sanity; without the outlet of resenting and avenging his wrongs in thought, he would become imbecile like 'the poor little mad woman that haunts the court.'

“The captain in the army being dead, she believed herself safe; but a
train of circumstances with which I need not trouble you led to
discovery. As I received the story, they began in an imprudence on
her own part one day when she was taken by surprise, which shows how
difficult it is for the firmest of us (she was very firm) to be
always guarded. There was great domestic trouble and amazement, you
may suppose; I leave you to imagine, Sir Leicester, the husband’s
grief. But that is not the present point. When Mr. Rouncewell’s
townsman heard of the disclosure, he no more allowed the girl to be
patronized and honoured than he would have suffered her to be trodden
underfoot before his eyes. Such was his pride, that he indignantly
took her away, as if from reproach and disgrace. He had no sense of
the honour done him and his daughter by the lady’s condescension; not
the least. He resented the girl’s position, as if the lady had been
the commonest of commoners. That is the story. I hope Lady Dedlock
will excuse its painful nature.”

“He come in at the door,” said the old man, slowly pointing an
imaginary track along the shop, “on the day he did it—the whole
neighbourhood had said for months before that he would do it, of a
certainty sooner or later—he come in at the door that day, and
walked along there, and sat himself on a bench that stood there, and
asked me (you’ll judge I was a mortal sight younger then) to fetch
him a pint of wine. ‘For,’ says he, ‘Krook, I am much depressed; my
cause is on again, and I think I’m nearer judgment than I ever was.’
I hadn’t a mind to leave him alone; and I persuaded him to go to the
tavern over the way there, t’other side my lane (I mean Chancery
Lane); and I followed and looked in at the window, and saw him,
comfortable as I thought, in the arm-chair by the fire, and company
with him. I hadn’t hardly got back here when I heard a shot go
echoing and rattling right away into the inn. I ran out—neighbours
ran out—twenty of us cried at once, ‘Tom Jarndyce!’”
c5:p58.summary: Krook describes in vivid detail Tom Jarndyce's final day: how he came into the shop depressed, asked for wine, was persuaded to go to a tavern, and then shot himself. The neighbourhood had long predicted this tragedy.

forlorn man could have been prophetically seen lying here by the
mother at whose breast he nestled, a little child, with eyes upraised
